description.narrative: Currently, DRM in Uganda is largely characterized by inequitable tax policies and practices that promote the interests of thecorporations and the rich at the expense of the poor and marginalised.There is limited capacity of government institutions (i.e.,Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, UgandaRevenue Authority, and Local Governments) to equitably broaden the narrow tax base. This is because the legal and policyframework is still skewed towards attracting foreign direct investment, which encourages overreliance on taxes such as personalincome tax, VAT and excise duty which has increased the tax burden on the same categories of people hence perpetuatinginequality.The framework also promotes tax incentives and exemptions despite the lack of clear guidelines for the granting of such incentivesand lack of cost-benefit analysis conducted. The country has also greatly suffered from revenue loss through IFFs in the form oftax avoidance and evasion as well as corruption.IFFs have been facilitated by the “race to the bottom” through tax incentives and exemptions in the region and have also beenfacilitated by the adoption of harmful double taxation agreements (DTAs). For example, the Panama Papers leak (2016) revealedhow Heritage Oil Company decided a month after the execution of its Sale and Purchase Agreement with Tullow Oil to move itsdomicile from Bahamas to Mauritius with a view of avoiding paying capital gains tax using the DTA between Uganda andMauritius.In the extractives sector, the legal frameworks provide limited transparency. The counties that host mining operations generallybenefit too little from the extraction despite the need for public investments to better the lives of citizens and to finance a justenergy transition.The challenges of DRM have been exacerbated by the limited engagement ofrights-holders in revenue mobilization andaccountability processes. The contributing factors include the limited capacity of key stakeholders to participate in policyformulation processes atdifferent levels. There is little public understanding of the nexus between DRM, service delivery,democratic governance, and their role in grassroots policy formation.The allocation and utilization of the mobilized revenue in many instances has also frustrated DRM efforts in Uganda as there areconcerns around efficiency of spending andelite capture of public budgets.There are also limited spaces for citizen engagement in the formulation of tax policies. This is partly attributable to the fact thatprocesses have remained a domain of a few government officials and experts who have also not had commitment to mainstreamrecommendations of key policy guidelines. This limits citizens’ appreciation of the need for citizens to pay taxes to enablegovernment to raise revenue.There are also weak CSO platforms and alliances for engagement of different stakeholders including citizens, the CSOs andgovernment on issues related to DRM. Currently, SEATINI Uganda hosts and coordinates the Tax JusticeAlliance, which is aloose coalition of 43 CSOs whose objective is to mobilise citizens to influence fair, progressive and accountable tax policies, andpractices in Uganda. However, the network has several CSOs who need to build their capacity to be able to effectively promotefiscal justice.

participating-org.narrative:
The Southern and Eastern African Trade, Information and Negotiations Institute (SEATINI) Uganda is a regional non-governmental organisation founded in 1996 soon after the WTO Singapore Ministerial Conference. It happened when people realised that Africa in particular and Third World countries in general were marginalised in the World Trade Organisation's negotiations. SEATINI was formed to enhance the capacity in these negotiations of African trade officials and negotiators through technical assistance,and also through extending the trade debate to other stakeholders, especially civil society organisations, the media and parliaments. SEATINI also brings together African trade officials and negotiators, with a purpose of consolidating Africa's negotiating positions.
SEATINI was born when it was observed that: - African public policy in international forums is often determined ad hoc, and African governments are mostly takers, not makers, of international decisions that affect people's lives. Governments often sign international trade agreements without adequate information or analysis. Alternatively, the lack of a clear perception of their interests, they often resort to a simple negative posture rather than make commitments to agreements that mightbe of value to them; - the private sector is equally badly informed about the challenges of globalisation and the effect of the multilateral trading regime; - civil society understands the complexities of the international regime but it is often excludedfrom decision-making, both at home and in international forums.
Presently, the organisation has offices in Harare, Johannesburg, Kampala, Nairobi and Geneva. The Uganda office was established in 2001 and is fully registered with the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The country chapters are semi-autonomous with the country director responsible for reporting to the regional director in Zimbabwe. SEATINI has one board for the whole organisation.
ON THE FINANCE FOR DEVELOPMENT PROJECT: SEATINI Uganda is leading the implementation of Tax Justice interventions in Uganda at national level. This is aimed at influencing fair tax policy reform in Uganda at national level and closely works with other national and subnational level F4D partners.
